blocks.text: Reflection prompts here apply the reflection idea continuously across an agent whole multi-step trajectory, checking whether each action actually succeeded and whether overall progress is genuinely being made, distinct from the earlier Reflection Prompting topic, which covered a single attempt, feedback, retry cycle.

This topic covers how agent-level reflection differs from that earlier single-cycle technique, checking whether an action actually succeeded, assessing overall progress toward a goal, how reflection triggers plan revision, and the real risk of reflecting so much that an agent never makes forward progress.
1. Reflection Within an Ongoing Agent Loop

blocks.alt: Building on planning prompts, reflection prompts add an ongoing trajectory self check

blocks.text: Reflection in an agent context means the agent periodically checking in on its own progress across an entire multi-step task, not just once after a single failed attempt, but continuously as it works through a longer trajectory of actions.
2. This Topic vs the Earlier Reflection Prompting Topic

blocks.alt: Reflection prompting covered one attempt, feedback, and retry, reflection prompts here apply continuously across a whole trajectory

blocks.text: The earlier Reflection Prompting topic, covered in the Advanced Prompting Techniques module, described a single loop, attempt a task, get real feedback, reflect, retry, reflection prompts in an agent context extend this same underlying idea across an entire multi-step trajectory, potentially reflecting after every single action rather than only at the end of one complete attempt.

blocks.text: 3. Reflecting on Whether an Action Actually Succeeded

blocks.alt: An action gets taken, followed by checking whether it actually succeeded, producing a reflection answer

blocks.text: After each action, an agent can explicitly reflect on whether that specific action actually produced the intended result, a tool call that returns an error, or a result that does not match what was expected, needs this reflection step to be caught rather than proceeding as if the action had genuinely succeeded.

code.content:
result = execute_tool(action)
reflection_prompt = (
    f"The action returned: {result}. Did this action succeed as intended? "
    "If not, what went wrong and what should happen next?"
)

blocks.text: 4. Reflecting on Overall Progress Toward the Goal

blocks.alt: After several steps completed, the agent asks whether it is actually making progress toward the goal

blocks.text: Beyond checking individual actions, periodic reflection on the bigger picture, "given everything done so far, am I genuinely closer to completing the original goal," catches a subtler failure mode, a sequence of individually successful actions that nonetheless are not actually converging on the intended outcome.
5. Reflection Triggering Plan Revision

blocks.alt: Reflection revealing a problem leads to the plan getting revised

blocks.text: This connects directly back to the previous topic, planning prompts, when reflection reveals a genuine problem, an action failed, progress has stalled, this is exactly the trigger for the dynamic re-planning covered there, reflection and planning work together as a connected pair within the agent loop.

blocks.title: Reflection without a mechanism to act on it accomplishes little
blocks.content: Reflecting on a problem is only useful if the agent system actually feeds that reflection back into revising its plan or next action, reflection prompts and planning prompts need to be wired together, not treated as isolated, disconnected steps.

blocks.text: 6. Reflection Frequency, After Every Step vs Periodically

blocks.alt: Reflecting after every single step is compared against reflecting periodically or at key points

blocks.text: Reflecting after every single action provides the most thorough monitoring but adds a model call, and therefore cost and latency, at every single step, reflecting only periodically, or at points genuinely likely to reveal a problem, trades some monitoring thoroughness for meaningfully lower overhead.
7. A Worked Example of Agent Self-Reflection

An agent working through a multi-step data gathering task completes three of five planned steps, a periodic reflection check reveals that the data gathered so far does not actually cover what the original goal required, prompting a plan revision before continuing rather than completing the remaining two steps of an already misdirected plan.
8. The Risk of Reflecting Too Much

blocks.alt: Excessive reflection leads to wasted cycles and indecision

blocks.text: An agent that reflects too frequently, or too critically, on every minor detail can end up spending more cycles second-guessing itself than actually making forward progress, a genuinely well tuned reflection frequency catches real problems without creating this kind of unproductive indecision loop.
9. Reflection and Agent Evaluation

This connects directly to agent evaluation, covered in the closing topic of this module, tracking how often reflection actually catches a genuine problem, versus how often it triggers unnecessary plan churn, is itself a useful signal for evaluating whether an agent reflection strategy is well calibrated.
Worked Example

A developer builds a research agent that executes its full five step plan without any intermediate reflection, only checking the final result, one early step silently returns incomplete data, and by the time this is discovered at the end, all four subsequent steps have built on that flawed foundation, requiring the entire task to restart.

Adding reflection after each step, specifically checking whether the returned data actually looks complete and usable before proceeding, catches the same incomplete data issue immediately after the first step, allowing the agent to retry just that one step rather than discovering the problem only after the entire trajectory had already gone astray.
Common Mistakes

items: Only checking final results at the end of a long trajectory instead of reflecting at intermediate points
Reflecting without any mechanism to actually act on what the reflection reveals, wiring reflection to nothing
Reflecting after every single minor action, adding unnecessary cost and latency without a proportional benefit
Confusing this continuous, trajectory-level reflection with the single attempt-feedback-retry cycle from the earlier Reflection Prompting topic

blocks.text: Practice

Take a multi-step agent task you have designed or could design, decide at which specific points reflection would genuinely be valuable versus unnecessary overhead, and write a reflection prompt for one of those points that checks both action success and overall progress toward the goal.
Key Takeaway

Reflection prompts in an agent context apply the reflection idea continuously across a full multi-step trajectory, checking whether individual actions actually succeeded and whether overall progress toward the goal is genuine, feeding directly into plan revision when a problem surfaces, and requiring a carefully calibrated frequency to catch real problems without creating unproductive indecision.
